item.title: Insolation-forced oceanic changes triggered the Eurasian Ice Sheet collapse and the Last Termination
item.dc:creator: Dong Wu, Siqi Li, Jón Eiríksson, Esther Ruth Guðmundsdóttir, Yair Rosenthal, Ningjing Hu, … (+3)
item.description:
Nature Communications — matched: ice sheet, ice shelf, Eurasian ice sheet, NH ice sheets, meltwater, iceberg, ocean circulation, deglaciation, last glacial maximum, insolation, Quaternary, climate feedback
Abstract The collapse of Northern Hemisphere ice sheets has been deemed as a trigger for the chain of positive climate feedback during glacial terminations in Quaternary. Increasing boreal summer insolation is considered the ultimate driver of their collapse, however, the initiating mechanisms remain elusive. Here we report an unambiguous warming trend in the southern Nordic Seas, which coincides with the initial phase of Northern Hemisphere summer insolation increase at the end of the Last Glacial Maximum. A subsequent phase of surface cooling is observed, closely corresponding to the massive freshwater discharge attributed to the meltwater pulse at 19ka BP. Our reconstructions demonstrate that the initial collapse of Northern Hemisphere ice sheets during the Last Termination occurred in Eurasian Ice Sheet, driven by a chain of oceanic responses to the insolation increase. Specifically, increasing boreal insolation induced a northward migration of the mid-latitude Westerlies under a positive NAO phase, promoting poleward oceanic heat transport and hence subsequent warming in Nordic Seas, thereby accelerating the ablation of the marine-based Eurasian Ice Shelves. This led to a catastrophic release of icebergs into Nordic Seas, eventually triggering a series of ocean circulation feedbacks that further promoted the deglaciation.

item.title: On the Fidelity of Oxygen Isotope‐Based Sea Level Reconstructions: A Case Study of Marine Isotope Stage 3
item.dc:creator: Tamara Pico, Jesse R. Farmer, Sarah A. Shackleton, Robert K. Poirier, Bradley R. Markle, L. E. Lisiecki
item.description:
Paleoceanography and Paleoclimatology — matched: ice sheet, last glacial maximum, glacial cycle, marine isotope stage, MIS stage, proxy, oxygen isotope, glacial isostatic adjustment, GIA, sea level
Abstract Although foraminiferal oxygen isotope records (δ 18 O F ) have long been used to develop time‐continuous estimates of past global ice volume, growing evidence indicates that the ice volume and temperature contributions to δ 18 O F diverge considerably over the last glacial cycle. Across Marine Isotope Stage 3 (MIS 3; 57 to 29 ka), estimates of peak global sea level based on δ 18 O F are ∼30 m lower than reconstructions based on recent glacial geology, geologic sea‐level records, and glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA) modeling approaches. Here we address this mismatch by quantifying uncertainties in converting δ 18 O F to global sea level during MIS 3. We review the geochemical tools to assess the contributions of ocean temperature, diagenesis, and the isotopic composition of ice sheets to δ 18 O F records across MIS 3. We show that recent advances in our understanding of these and other factors that contribute uncertainty (e.g., global sea level during the Last Glacial Maximum) help to explain the MIS 3 gap between global sea level estimates based on δ 18 O F and GIA analyses of geologic sea‐level records. We find that the accuracy and precision of MIS 3 ocean temperature reconstructions is likely a key contributor, and various MIS 3 temperature reconstructions can reduce the “gap” by 30%–70% (∼10–20 m). Future improvements in the precision of temperature reconstructions will better constrain the ice volume component of δ 18 O F records. Ultimately, assessing the fidelity of δ 18 O F as a proxy for global ice volume is key to disentangling the feedbacks between climate and ice sheets over the Pleistocene.

item.title: Antarctic sea ice response to meltwater due to Antarctic ice sheet mass loss in a multi-model ensemble
item.dc:creator: Andrew G. Pauling, Inga J. Smith, Torge Martin, Jeff K. Ridley, David P. Stevens, Max Thomas, … (+8)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, Antarctic, meltwater, mass loss, sea ice, Southern Ocean, ensemble
Climate models typically do not include meltwater entering the Southern Ocean due to Antarctic ice sheet mass loss. Previous work shows this meltwater drives sea ice growth, but the varying responses have been difficult to compare across models. We ran 11 climate models using the same meltwater input and found a wide range of sea ice responses depending on the background state in each model. Understanding this uncertainty in response is important for future projections of Antarctic sea ice.

item.title: Transition of Glacial Regimes Recorded at IODP Site U1524 in the Ross Sea, Antarctica, Over the Last 800 Thousand Years
item.dc:creator: James Marschalek, Tina van de Flierdt, Molly O. Patterson, Georgia Grant, S J Kim, Wenshen Xiao, … (+21)
item.description:
Paleoceanography and Paleoclimatology — matched: ice sheet, Antarctic, Antarctica, West Antarctic, sea ice, last glacial maximum, interglacial, marine isotope stage, MIS stage, proxy, foraminifera, climate change
Abstract Reconstructing past interactions between the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) and changing environmental conditions in the Ross Sea region can help determine long‐term WAIS stability. Existing sedimentary records reveal changes to oceanography, sea ice and ice sheet extent over the glacial‐interglacial cycles of the last ∼800 kyr. There are, however, few high‐resolution, ice‐proximal records extending to before the Last Glacial Maximum. Here, we examine a broad suite of lithological, biogenic, physical property and geochemical data from International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Site U1524 from the continental rise in the central Ross Sea. An age model spanning the last ∼800 kyr is established within constraints provided by biostratigraphy, palaeomagnetism and foraminifera amino acid racemization. Lithofacies analysis reveals the pattern of glacial advance and interglacial retreat. Enhanced delivery of ice rafted debris and preservation of radiolaria occurs during deglacial and interglacial periods, with fine‐grained diatom‐bearing to diatom‐rich sediments deposited during glacial periods. Foraminifera are preserved during the latest parts of the Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 11 and 9 interglacials. Proxy data apparently suggest higher productivity during glacial periods, which is explained by reworking and redeposition of older detritus from the continental shelf. A change in the character of glacial period sediments after MIS 7 (∼200 kyr ago) suggests there was a less extensive grounded ice sheet during the last two glacial periods. Together, these results provide a detailed reconstruction of mid‐ to late‐Pleistocene ocean–ice sheet interactions, improving understanding of how the Ross Sea region may respond to ongoing climate change.

item.title: legoESM: a modular, differentiable, multiscale, AI-ready Earth system model built with AI agents
item.dc:creator: Pierre Gentine, Dhruv Balwada, Ayta\c{c} Pa\c{c}al, Linnia Hawkins, Alistair Adcroft, Hang Fan, … (+9)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: data assimilation, Earth system model, Earth system, greenhouse gas, numerical method, parameterization, emulator
arXiv:2610.11883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Earth system models (ESMs) have grown tremendously in realism, yet key uncertainties persist in the climate response to greenhouse-gas forcing, particularly due to cloud radiative feedbacks. In addition, their software architecture was not designed for accelerator hardware or modern artificial intelligence (AI). Here we present legoESM, a composable, differentiable, multiscale ESM written in JAX. It builds on decades of community-developed parameterizations and numerical methods, recast in a unified framework by AI coding agents under a human-specified scientific contract and verified through benchmarking. Dynamical cores, physics schemes, grids, complexity levels and components are swappable like building blocks, and can use conventional physics or machine-learned emulators. A single code base spans metre-scale large-eddy simulation to global simulations and weather to climate. End-to-end differentiability enables gradient-based calibration, variational data assimilation and online training. legoESM modular architecture enables systematic evaluation of diverse model variants to explore structural uncertainty and test hypotheses. legoESM produces realistic simulations across scales, reduces land-surface temperature bias through gradient-based calibration, and scales efficiently on GPUs to kilometer-scale simulations. It offers an open, community infrastructure for hypothesis testing, research and teaching in Earth sciences and a template for multiscale physical systems.

item.title: Cryosphere hazards under weather and climate extremes in the Hindu Kush Himalaya: The cryosphere hazard interaction pathways (CHiP) framework
item.dc:creator: Mohd. Farooq Azam, Sachin Kumar Thakur, Sher Muhammad, Himanshu Kaushik, Ashim Sattar, Saswata Sanyal
item.description:
Progress in Disaster Science — matched: cryosphere, glacier, permafrost, climate extreme, climate change
The Hindu Kush Himalaya has emerged as a hotspot of cryosphere hazards due to climate change. While long-term warming governs glacier, snow, and permafrost evolution, weather and climate extremes (WCEs) often control hazard timing and magnitude. However, understanding of WCEs–cryosphere interactions remain limited and existing preconditioning-triggering concepts have examined WCEs impact on cryosphere components in isolation rather than applying a single framework. Here, we synthesize recent evidence and propose the Cryosphere Hazard Interaction Pathways (CHiP) Framework under WCEs. The framework links WCEs to cryosphere hazards via direct triggering (P1), indirect or lagged response (P2). These pathways drive compound and cascading hazards across the region. Integrating CHiP under WCEs into monitoring, hazard investigation, and early warning is essential for improving multi-hazard risk assessment and climate-resilient adaptation in high-mountain regions.

item.title: A long-term trend toward wetter conditions during MIS 2 inferred from modern-monitoring-based stalagmite multi-proxy records from Remi Cave, Central China
item.dc:creator: Yiping Tian, Yunxia Li, Zhimao Ye, Hanying Li, Youfeng Ning, Liangcheng Tan, … (+2)
item.description:
Quaternary Science Reviews — matched: sea surface temperature, marine isotope stage, MIS stage, proxy
The ongoing debate regarding the spatial pattern of precipitation and effective moisture changes in monsoonal eastern China during the Marine Isotope Stage 2 (MIS 2) centers on the hydroclimatic evolution of the middle and lower Yangtze River Valley. Here, we present an approximately four-year (December 2020 to December 2024) systematic modern monitoring program and multi-proxy records (δ 18 O, δ 13 C, Mg/Ca, Sr/Ca, Ba/Ca) from stalagmite RM4 in Remi cave, Hunan Province, Central China, spanning ∼25.7‒14.5 kyr BP. Based on modern monitoring results and cross-validation among multi-proxy records, the δ 13 C values and Sr/Ca and Ba/Ca ratios in the stalagmite RM4 record are interpreted as qualitative indicators of an integrated effective-moisture signal, whereas variations in RM4 δ 18 O appear to be mainly associated with large-scale atmospheric circulation. During the ∼25.7–14.5 kyr BP interval, the δ 13 C, Sr/Ca, and Ba/Ca records from stalagmite RM4, complemented by various records from nearby stalagmites and peat bogs, indicate an overall long-term trend toward increased effective moisture in central China. This trend is consistent with precipitation reconstructions from northeastern China, but contrasts with contemporaneous long-term drying trends reported in northern and southern China, which may point to a quadrupole-like pattern of hydroclimatic change across monsoonal eastern China. We suggest that this marked spatial heterogeneity in hydroclimate may have been modulated by zonal sea surface temperature gradients across the tropical Pacific, which may have influenced the position and intensity of the West Pacific subtropical high and possibly triggered a cyclonic anomaly to its north through the western North Pacific anomalous anticyclone. Our results highlight the value of integrating modern cave monitoring, with multi-proxy records from various archives for understanding the controlling mechanisms of stalagmite proxy records.

item.title: Biological pump variations in the northeastern Indian Ocean since the last glaciation: evidence from coccolithophores
item.dc:creator: Nilufar Yasmin Liza, Xiang Su, Chuanxiu Luo, Lanlan Zhang, Sui Wan, Rong Xiang
item.description:
Journal of Micropalaeontology — matched: deglaciation, last glacial maximum, interglacial, Holocene, sediment core, sea level, carbon cycle
The biological pump (BP) constitutes a key component of the global carbon cycle by mediating the export of organic carbon from the surface ocean to the deep sea. However, long-term variability of BP strength in the northeastern Indian Ocean (NEIO), particularly within the strongly stratified Bay of Bengal (BoB), remains inadequately constrained due to the complex interplay between monsoon forcing and freshwater-induced stratification. Here, we present a high-resolution reconstruction of BP variability over the last ∼ 53 kyr based on primary productivity (PP) estimates derived from quantitative analyses of coccolithophore assemblages in a sediment core from the southern BoB. Coccoliths are abundant and well preserved throughout the record, with assemblages dominated by Florisphaera profunda , Gephyrocapsa oceanica , and Emiliania huxleyi . The reconstructed PP record exhibits pronounced glacial–interglacial (G–IG) variability, characterized by reduced productivity during the Last Glacial Maximum, followed by a progressive increase during the deglaciation and a peak in the Early Holocene. Principal component analysis of productivity records across the Indian Ocean (IO) identifies G–IG climate variability as the dominant mode of basin-scale productivity change while distinguishing secondary atmospheric and hydrological controls on regional productivity. Comparison with PP records from other sectors of the IO further highlights marked spatial heterogeneity in BP responses to basin-scale climatic forcing. In the NEIO, productivity was primarily controlled by G–IG changes in upper-ocean stratification and nutrient availability driven by sea level fluctuations and freshwater forcing, whereas secondary variability reflects the distinct atmospheric and hydrological expressions of the Indian Summer Monsoon. Our findings indicate that regional hydrographic processes governed the expression of basin-scale climatic forcing, distinguishing the freshwater-controlled NEIO from the wind-driven upwelling systems of the western tropical IO.

item.title: Deep learning in the abyss: a stratified Physics Informed Neural Network for data assimilation
item.dc:creator: Vadim Limousin, Nelly Pustelnik, Bruno Deremble, Antoine Venaille
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: data assimilation, machine learning, neural network
arXiv:2503.19160v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The reconstruction of deep ocean currents is a major challenge in data assimilation due to the scarcity of interior data. In this work, we present a proof of concept for deep ocean flow reconstruction using a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), a machine learning approach that offers an alternative to traditional data assimilation methods. We introduce an efficient algorithm called StrAssPINN (for Stratified Assimilation PINNs), which assigns a separate network to each layer of the ocean model while allowing them to interact during training. The neural network takes spatiotemporal coordinates as input and predicts the velocity field at those points. Using a SIREN architecture (a multilayer perceptron with sine activation functions), which has proven effective in various contexts, the network is trained using both available observational data and dynamical priors enforced at several collocation points. We apply this method to pseudo-observed ocean data generated from a 3-layer quasi-geostrophic model, where the pseudo-observations include surface-level data akin to SWOT observations of sea surface height, interior data similar to ARGO floats, and a limited number of deep ARGO-like measurements in the lower layers. Our approach successfully reconstructs ocean flows in both the interior and surface layers, demonstrating a strong ability to resolve key ocean mesoscale features, including vortex rings, eastward jets associated with potential vorticity fronts, and smoother Rossby waves. This work serves as a prelude to applying StrAssPINN to real-world observational data.

item.title: A Graph Neural Network for Global Daily Fire Radiative Power Prediction at Medium-Range Lead Times
item.dc:creator: Li Zhang, Jun Wang, Isidora Jankov, Yongxin Liu, Gonzalo A. Ferrada, Ravan Ahmadov, … (+3)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: predictability, reanalysis, neural network
arXiv:2610.11022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Skillful prediction of biomass-burning activity several days in advance is important for air-quality forecasting and aerosol prediction. Two operational constraints motivate this work. First, the GBBEPx satellite fire radiative power (FRP) product used to initialize NOAA's GEFS-Aerosols is available with about a 1.5-day latency, so each forecast cycle relies on the most recently available, but already outdated, fire observations. Second, these fire inputs are then held fixed throughout the subsequent 5-day operational forecast, or 7 days in the GSL experimental system, effectively assuming no evolution in fire activity. We develop a data-driven model that predicts global FRP one to seven days ahead from the most recent available observations. The model adapts a spatiotemporal graph neural network using reanalysis meteorology, land-cover and vegetation information, recent fire history, and GBBEPx FRP as the training target. It is trained on 2020-2022 data and evaluated for 2023-2024. The model reproduces the global seasonal cycle and substantially outperforms persistence. At 0.1$^\circ$ resolution, mean squared error is reduced by 32% at one-day lead and 43% at seven days in 2023, and by 24% and 40% in 2024. At 1$^\circ$ resolution, the critical success index ranges from 0.32 to 0.60. Detection skill declines only modestly with lead time, whereas intensity skill degrades more rapidly. Large fires are detected reliably, but their radiative power is systematically underestimated. These results demonstrate useful predictability of fire activity several days ahead and identify intensity calibration and small-fire placement as the main remaining challenges before predicted FRP can support operational aerosol forecasts.

item.title: Glacial lake outburst flood hazard and downstream impacts: lessons from Afghanistan examples
item.dc:creator: Fayezurahman Azizi, Ayoub Fatihi, Gilles Antoniazza, Matteo Bertolazzi, Rayees Ahmed, Stuart Nicholas Lane
item.description:
Natural Hazards — matched: englacial, glacier, remote sensing
Abstract Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) pose a growing risk in high mountain regions as climate-driven glacier retreat accelerates lake expansion and new lake formation. In the Hindu Kush Himalaya, particularly in Afghanistan, triggering processes and GLOF propagation downstream are largely unstudied. This study evaluates two Afghanistan GLOFs (Peshghor 2018; Bam-Tanab 2021) using field observations and satellite imagery, and applies two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulation (BASEMENT-MD with BASEbreach) to the Kunj-Peshghor lake event to assess flood propagation, dam-breach dynamics, and downstream hazards under different scenarios. Both lakes formed and expanded over 33–42 days before catastrophic drainage, triggered by extreme temperatures, rapid-melt, ice-cliff collapse, and englacial tunnel failure. Both impacted Peshghor village downstream. The Kunj-Peshghor lake flood wave produced estimated peak velocities of 9 ms −1 and depths >10 m in confined valleys, associated with peak discharges >170 m 3 s −1 , high turbidity >800 NTU, and channel widening of up to 250 m. Secondary surges caused by temporary river blockages prolonged flooding and amplified downstream impacts. Hazard mapping indicates that ~46% of inundated zones in the Peshghor village fell within high to very high hazard levels, threatening settlements, roads, markets, and agricultural land. These findings provide the first quantitative GLOF propagation modeling for Afghanistan and highlight the need for site-specific monitoring, early warning systems, and mitigation measures. Both GLOFs were caused by the rapid formation and expansion of new lakes. This raises the question about whether current approaches to identifying dangerous lakes, based on remote-sensing of existing lakes are sufficient to detect all dangerous lakes and the associated hazards.

item.title: Spatiotemporal Assessment of Baltoro Glacier Snow-Cover Dynamics: Relevance to Indus Basin Water Resources and Irrigation
item.dc:creator: Osama Abbasi, Hajra Hassan, Syeda Zubia Naqvi, Ghulam Mujtaba, Raja Umer Sajjad
item.description:
Jammu Kashmir Journal of Agriculture — matched: glacier, meltwater
Glaciers of the Karakoram feed the Upper Indus, whose meltwater supports one of the largest irrigation systems in the world and, through it, the soils and crops of Pakistan. This study assessed the change in snow-covered surface of Baltoro Glacier between 2000 and 2020 and tested its relationship with temperature and precipitation. Landsat 5, 7 and 8 imagery was classified with the Normalized Difference Snow Index (NDSI) in ArcGIS, and climate data (2000-2020) were obtained from NASA POWER (MERRA-2) for the glacier grid cell (35.92° N, 74.30° E; mean elevation 3,627 m). Snow-covered area declined by 9 percentage points between December 2000 and December 2020 and by 13 percentage points between August 2000 and August 2020 (mean 11). Annual loss increased significantly through time (0.041% yr⁻¹; r = 0.79, p < 0.001) and averaged 0.30% yr⁻¹ in 2000-2012 compared with 0.89% yr⁻¹ in 2013–2020. Simple linear regression showed positive but statistically non-significant associations of snow-cover loss with temperature (R² = 0.034, p = 0.43) and precipitation (R² = 0.056, p = 0.30). The modest overall loss is consistent with the Karakoram anomaly and the insulating effect of supraglacial debris, whereas the late-period acceleration warrants monitoring because changes in glacier snow cover may have implications for downstream water resources, including irrigation, soil moisture and salinity management.

item.title: Can we define climate by means of an ensemble? A tale of time scales of convergence
item.dc:creator: Gábor Drótos, Tamás Bódai
item.description:
Earth System Dynamics — matched: ensemble
Climate and its change is of central importance to science and human society in general. However, it appears to us that a satisfactory definition of climate has not yet appeared in the literature. We attempt to introduce one which is based on an ensemble of realizations and satisfies uniqueness. Within this framework, it also attends to different time scales of relevance, a well-established treatment of which is the main novelty of our work.

item.title: From concept to action: Driving impact through responsible research practices in the International Polar Year 2032–2033 An early career perspective
item.dc:creator: Samuel G. Hartharn-Evans, Chloe Nunn, Amy Macfarlane, Natalia Banega, Anna Belcher, Radiance Calmer, … (+5)
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: polar
by Samuel G. Hartharn-Evans, Chloe Nunn, Amy Macfarlane, Natalia Banega, Anna Belcher, Radiance Calmer, Svenja Holste, Louise Mercer, Ningning Sun, M. A. J. van Soest, Zoe Wright Regions at the poles are warming at rates two to four times higher than the global average, driving profound environmental, societal, and geopolitical changes. As Polar Early Career Researchers with careers extending into and beyond the 5th International Polar Year in 2032–2033, we have a responsibility to shape research practices that are impactful, ethical, and sustainable. We argue that current definitions of research impact often prioritize narrow, quantifiable metrics, overlooking cultural, environmental, and long-term consequences. Building on interdisciplinary workshops held in 2025 at the Polar Early Career World Summit (USA) and the Centre for Ecology and Hydrology (UK), this paper redefines research impact for polar science and presents tangible action for integrating responsible practices ahead of the next IPY. We outline priorities across three levels: 1) individual researchers, who should practice reflexivity, promote interdisciplinarity, and implement environmentally responsible methods; 2) regional and national institutions, which must provide equitable funding, training, and inclusive protocols; 3) international IPY planning bodies, which should strengthen communication, publish guidelines, and implement regulations to prevent exploitative practices. Our call to action emphasizes collaboration, transparency, and improved impact evaluation frameworks to ensure that polar research delivers societal and environmental benefits while minimizing unintended consequences. This vision begins now and extends beyond the IPY, offering a roadmap for responsible polar science.

item.title: Strategic Governance of AI Models in Earth Science
item.dc:creator: Makoto Kelp, Amirhossein Arzani, Patricia Castellanos, Paul Griffiths, Ivan Higuera-Mendieta, Manuel Perez-Carrasco, … (+3)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: emulator
arXiv:2610.10560v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI foundation models pretrained on weather and climate data are increasingly fine-tuned to Earth science tasks well beyond weather forecasting. Their development and adoption are outpacing the scientific community's ability to evaluate them. These models are judged almost entirely by benchmark skill metrics, which measure how closely a forecast reproduces a reference product but not whether a model represents the physical processes governing the system it predicts. Forecast skill and physical reliability are therefore distinct properties. The distinction is most consequential under the nonstationary conditions of a changing climate for which these models were never trained. We identify five priorities for the physical evaluation of AI models in Earth science from task-specific emulators to foundation models, spanning training data, fine-tuning, behavioral testing, mechanistic interpretability, and output validation. We recommend three activities for the coming decade: 1) open AI-ready evaluation datasets, 2) a shared reporting standard for physics-based evaluation, and 3) a dedicated research program on the safety of these models.

item.title: Climate changes in hydrometeorological parameters of the Varzob river basin in the period 1980–2020
item.dc:creator: Nomvar Kurbon, Rukhshona Ibrogimova, Ozodbakht Sadriddinov, Bekhruz Shonazarov
item.description:
Sustainable Development of Mountain Territories — matched: glaciology, climate change
Introduction. Climate of Tajikistan is shaped by geographic location, complex topography, elevation, atmospheric circulation, and surface characteristics. It is marked by aridity, intense heat, and strong seasonal variation in temperature, humidity, precipitation, and solar radiation. Average annual temperatures range from +17 °C in the south to −6 °C and below in the east; absolute extremes reach −63 °C (Eastern Pamirs) and +48 °C (southwest). Annual precipitation varies from 70-160 mm in lowland and highland deserts to over 1800 mm in the central part of the country. The study examines temperature and precipitation changes (1991-2018) and snow cover dynamics (2005-2020) on the southern slopes of the Gissar Range. The analysis covers changes in meteorological conditions and their impact on the hydrological regime of the Varzob River over two periods: 1981-2000 and 2001-2020. Purpose of the research. To determine changes in meteorological conditions of the Varzob River basin and their impact on the river's hydrological regime over the last two decades of the 20th century (1981-2020) and the first two decades of the 21st century (2001-2020). Materials and Methods. Meteorological data from the Agency for Hydrometeorology of Tajikistan (TMS-84 monthly records) were used. Data were processed in MS Excel; trends were identified by the least square’s method using linear equations (y = ax + b) for temperature and precipitation, and a four-variable polynomial trend (y = ax⁴ + bx³ + cx² + dx + f) for river discharge. Terrain analysis was performed using SRTM imagery and QGIS. Results. 1. In 2001-2020 vs. 1981-2000, mean annual temperature rose by 0.3 °C in Dushanbe, 0.8 °C in Khushyary, and 1.5 °C in Maikhura; at Anzob it decreased by −0.1 °C. 2. Mean annual precipitation for 1981-2020: Anzob – 455.7 mm, Maikhura – 1057.2 mm, Khushyary – 1263.7 mm, Dushanbe – 598.9 mm. A decreasing precipitation trend was observed throughout the Varzob Gorge. 3. Seasonal precipitation (1981-2020): Anzob – 459.3 mm, Maikhura – 1059 mm, Khushyary – 1263.6 mm, Dushanbe – 604.9 mm. In highland areas ~70% of annual precipitation falls in winter and spring; in the basin interior – 75%; in Dushanbe – 80%. 4. Mean annual discharge of the Varzob River: 47.4 m3/s (1981-2000) and 48.9 m3/s (2001-2020), an increase of 1.5 m3/s. 5. The correlation between annual precipitation and mean annual temperature is very weak at all stations (strongest at Anzob, r = 0.025). The strongest precipitation–runoff correlation is between Khushyary station and Dakhana post (r = 0.582); the weakest temperature–runoff correlation is between Maikhura station and Dakhana post (r = −0.239). Resume. Analysis of long-term hydrometeorological data shows that in 2001-2020, compared with 1981-2000, mean annual temperature and river discharge tended to increase, while annual precipitation declined. Interannual correlation between precipitation and temperature is very weak across the basin; the precipitation–discharge correlation is stronger than the temperature–discharge correlation. Suggestions for practical applications and directions for future research. The findings can be applied to climate change research, glaciology, snow cover assessment, water resource management, and regional climate studies.

item.title: Adaptive observation weighting in TCKF1D-Var for ground-based multi-sensor thermodynamic retrievals prior to nocturnal heavy precipitation over China
item.dc:creator: Qi Zhang, Tianmeng Chen, Jianping Guo, Bin Deng, Han Li, Yu Wu
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
This study presents an adaptive observation-weighting scheme for thermodynamic profile retrievals from ground-based microwave radiometers and Mie–Raman lidars. The method dynamically estimates observational contributions during the retrieval process, replacing the commonly used static weighting assumption. Evaluation using 107 heavy-precipitation cases shows improved retrieval accuracy, particularly for atmospheric moisture profiles.
